questions.q: What is the primary difference between traditional rule-based programming and Machine Learning?
options: Rule-based programs are always faster
In ML, the system learns patterns from data instead of following manually written rules
ML only works with images, not text
ML requires more storage space
questions.explanation: Machine Learning shifts from humans writing every rule by hand to systems learning patterns directly from examples in data.

questions.q: A spam filter that checks 'if the email contains the word lottery, mark it as spam' is an example of what approach?
options: A neural network
Unsupervised learning
Reinforcement learning
A fixed, manually written rule
questions.explanation: This is a classic hand-written rule — the exact approach ML was designed to replace, since spammers could simply avoid flagged words.

questions.q: Which architecture, introduced in 2017, became the foundation for almost every modern LLM?
options: Decision Tree
Support Vector Machine
Transformer
Convolutional Neural Network
questions.explanation: The Transformer architecture, with its 'attention' mechanism, underlies nearly all modern large language models.

questions.q: What key mechanism does the Transformer architecture use to determine which words in a sentence are most relevant to each other?
options: Attention
Tokenization
Gradient descent
Backpropagation only
questions.explanation: Attention lets the model weigh which earlier words matter most when generating the next word, enabling coherent, context-aware output.

questions.q: In the sentence 'The dog chased the ball because it was fast,' what does the attention mechanism help the model correctly resolve?
options: That 'it' refers to the dog, not the ball
The temperature setting
The token count
The spelling of 'chased'
questions.explanation: Attention allows the model to correctly link pronouns and references to the right earlier word based on context.

questions.q: A model's 'weights' or 'parameters' are best described as:
options: The millions or billions of internal numeric values adjusted during training that store what the model learned
The temperature setting for inference
The name of the algorithm used
The dataset used for training
questions.explanation: Weights/parameters are the internal numeric values a model tunes during training — they are what actually store its learned patterns.

questions.q: What does it mean when an LLM is described as having '7B' parameters?
options: It processes 7 billion tokens per second
It has 7 billion internal weight values
It was trained for 7 billion seconds
It cost 7 billion dollars to build
questions.explanation: Parameter count (e.g. 7B = 7 billion) refers to the number of learned weight values inside the model.

questions.q: What is 'fine-tuning' in the context of model training?
options: Taking an already-trained model and training it further on a smaller, specific dataset to specialize its behavior
Converting a model into a vector database
Adjusting the temperature setting at inference time
Deleting unused parameters from a model
questions.explanation: Fine-tuning specializes a general model for a specific task by continuing training on a smaller, targeted dataset.

questions.q: From a security perspective, why is fine-tuning data a meaningful attack surface?
options: Fine-tuning always makes models slower
Fine-tuning removes all guardrails automatically
Poisoned fine-tuning data can plant hidden backdoors in the model's behavior
Fine-tuning data is never stored anywhere
questions.explanation: If an attacker can influence the fine-tuning dataset, they can implant hidden triggers or backdoors that affect the model's future behavior.

questions.q: What is 'inference' in the context of a deployed AI model?
options: Deleting a model after it is no longer needed
Measuring the loss function during training
The process of collecting training data
Using an already-trained model to produce an answer to a new input
questions.explanation: Inference is when a trained model is actually used to generate a response — this is the stage almost every attack in AI security targets.

questions.q: Why do almost all AI security attacks target the inference stage rather than the training stage directly?
options: Because inference is always encrypted
Because training never involves any data
Because attackers cannot access APIs
Because inference is where untrusted input, including attacker input, directly reaches the model
questions.explanation: Inference is the point where regular users — and attackers — can directly interact with the model, making it the primary entry point for most attacks.

questions.q: What is a 'token' in the context of how LLMs process text?
options: A type of neural network layer
A unit of GPU memory
A small chunk of text, roughly ¾ of a word on average, that the model actually processes
A password used to access the model's API
questions.explanation: LLMs don't process whole words directly — they break text into smaller pieces called tokens, and every input/output is measured in tokens.

questions.q: Why might an attacker write 'p a s s w o r d' with spaces instead of 'password' when trying to bypass a content filter?
options: Because the model cannot read spaced text at all
Because splitting or spacing out a word can bypass filters that only check for exact, whole-word token matches
To make the request more polite
Because spaces make text load faster
questions.explanation: Tokenization quirks mean an unusual spacing or splitting of a flagged word can slip past filters designed to catch the exact whole-word string.

questions.q: What is the 'context window' of a language model?
options: The number of users who can query the model simultaneously
The time limit for a single API request
The maximum number of tokens a model can process or 'see' at once in a single conversation
The physical screen size used to display the chat
questions.explanation: The context window is the model's short-term memory limit — anything outside this token limit is effectively forgotten.

questions.q: In a very long conversation that exceeds a model's context window, what typically happens to the earliest messages?
options: They are permanently stored in a separate database automatically
They fall outside the window and are effectively forgotten by the model
They are converted into system prompts
They are automatically flagged as malicious
questions.explanation: Once a conversation exceeds the context window, the oldest content is pushed out and the model no longer 'sees' it.

questions.q: What is a 'system prompt'?
options: A setting that controls GPU temperature
A message typed by the end user
The final answer produced by the model
Hidden instructions given to the model before the user's message, defining its role, rules, and boundaries
questions.explanation: The system prompt is usually invisible to the end user and sets the model's role, rules, and behavioral boundaries.

questions.q: Why should real secrets like API keys or passwords never be placed inside a system prompt?
options: This information can potentially be leaked through the model's output
Models cannot process text containing numbers
System prompts are automatically deleted every hour
System prompts are limited to 10 characters
questions.explanation: A model's output can often be manipulated into revealing its system prompt, so embedded secrets risk exposure.

questions.q: What does the 'temperature' setting control in an LLM's output?
options: How random or predictable the model's output is
The size of the training dataset
The physical heat generated by GPU hardware
The number of tokens in the context window
questions.explanation: Temperature controls randomness — low temperature gives consistent, predictable output; high temperature gives more varied, creative output.

questions.q: Why might a low-temperature system be easier for an attacker to reliably exploit compared to a high-temperature one?
options: Low temperature only works with image models
Low temperature increases the context window size
Low temperature makes the model more deterministic, so a working exploit is more likely to reproduce consistently
Low temperature disables all security filters
questions.explanation: Because low-temperature output is more consistent and predictable, an attacker's crafted exploit is more likely to work the same way every time.

questions.q: What is the difference between zero-shot and few-shot prompting?
options: Zero-shot uses images, few-shot uses text only
Zero-shot asks a model to do a task with no examples; few-shot provides a couple of examples first to guide behavior
Zero-shot is always faster than few-shot regardless of content
There is no meaningful difference
questions.explanation: Zero-shot gives no examples; few-shot includes example(s) in the prompt to steer the model's response pattern.

questions.q: What is a 'few-shot jailbreak'?
options: A jailbreak that only works on models with no context window
A jailbreak that requires physical server access
A defense technique used to block prompt injection
Using example(s) inside a malicious prompt to 'teach' the model to imitate an unsafe response pattern
questions.explanation: By including a few crafted examples of the desired unsafe behavior, an attacker can guide the model to imitate that pattern in its next response.

questions.q: What does an 'epoch' refer to in model training?
options: A single prediction made during inference
A unit of measurement for embeddings
The moment a model is deployed to production
One complete pass of the entire training dataset through the model
questions.explanation: An epoch is one full pass through the entire training dataset during the training process.

questions.q: What is a 'loss function' used for during training?
options: To encrypt the model's weights
To count the number of tokens in a conversation
To generate the system prompt automatically
To measure how wrong the model's prediction was compared to the correct answer
questions.explanation: The loss function quantifies the gap between the model's prediction and the correct answer; training aims to shrink this value over time.

questions.q: What optimization method do models typically use to adjust their weights to reduce the loss function?
options: Context windowing
Prompt chaining
Token splitting
Gradient descent
questions.explanation: Gradient descent gradually adjusts a model's weights in the direction that reduces the loss function.

questions.q: What is 'overfitting'?
options: When a model refuses too many user requests
When a model is too large to run on standard hardware
When a model memorizes its training data too closely and performs poorly on new, unseen data
When a model's temperature setting is set to zero
questions.explanation: Overfitting occurs when a model learns the training data too specifically rather than generalizing, hurting performance on new data.

questions.q: Why is an overfit model a privacy concern from a security standpoint?
options: Overfit models are more likely to leak memorized training data verbatim, including private records
Overfitting always disables the system prompt
Overfit models run slower and leak GPU heat data
Overfit models cannot process any user input
questions.explanation: Because an overfit model has memorized specific training examples rather than general patterns, it's more likely to regurgitate exact private data it saw during training.

questions.q: What is 'underfitting'?
options: When training data is stored in a vector database
When a model's context window is too large
When a model has too many parameters
When a model performs poorly across the board because it failed to learn enough from the training data
questions.explanation: Underfitting is the opposite problem from overfitting — the model hasn't learned enough patterns to perform well even on familiar-style data.

questions.q: What does RLHF stand for, and what is it used for?
options: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback; used to align model behavior, such as staying polite and refusing harmful requests
Recursive Loss Handling Framework; used for debugging
Rapid Learning for High Frequency data; used for speeding up training
Random Layer Hidden Function; used to randomize model weights
questions.explanation: RLHF has human reviewers rate model responses, training the model to favor highly-rated responses — this stage largely shapes safety behavior.

questions.q: Which of these is a real, documented example of supervised learning?
options: A model generating random text with no training data at all
A spam filter trained on thousands of emails already labeled 'spam' or 'not spam'
A model finding customer segments with no labels provided
An AI learning to play a game purely through trial-and-error rewards
questions.explanation: Supervised learning uses labeled examples — spam/not-spam labels are a textbook example of this approach.

questions.q: In supervised learning, what happens if an attacker manages to poison the labeled training data (e.g. mislabeling spam as safe)?
options: The model automatically detects and corrects the mislabeling
The model learns the wrong pattern and makes incorrect decisions later
Nothing changes because labels don't affect training
The model stops training entirely
questions.explanation: Poisoned labels teach the model incorrect associations, directly corrupting its future decision-making on similar inputs.

questions.q: What defines unsupervised learning?
options: The model only works with pre-labeled spam emails
The model is given data with no correct answers attached and must find patterns or groupings on its own
The model requires a system prompt to function
The model receives a reward or penalty for every action it takes
questions.explanation: Unsupervised learning finds structure in unlabeled data, such as grouping customers by behavior without predefined categories.

questions.q: In unsupervised learning, how might an attacker exploit the lack of labels?
options: By encrypting the entire dataset
By increasing the context window size
By deleting the model's parameters
By hiding malicious activity inside a large, legitimate-looking group so it blends in and isn't flagged as unusual
questions.explanation: Since unsupervised systems group data by similarity without ground-truth labels, malicious activity can be camouflaged within a large legitimate cluster.

questions.q: What defines reinforcement learning?
options: The model takes actions and receives rewards or penalties, learning over many attempts which actions lead to better outcomes
The model is trained only on labeled spam/not-spam data
The model requires no training data whatsoever
The model only processes images, never text
questions.explanation: Reinforcement learning is a trial-and-reward process — the model learns which actions maximize reward over repeated attempts.

questions.q: Most modern LLMs are trained using which combination of learning approaches?
options: Only supervised learning
Only unsupervised learning with no other stages
Only reinforcement learning
A combination of unsupervised pre-training, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning (RLHF)
questions.explanation: Modern LLMs typically combine large-scale unsupervised pre-training, supervised fine-tuning, and RLHF-based alignment.

questions.q: A neural network's 'hidden layers' are best described as:
options: The layers between input and output that process data step by step, passing results forward
A separate database storing user passwords
Layers that are encrypted and cannot be inspected by anyone
Layers that only exist in reinforcement learning models
questions.explanation: Hidden layers sit between the input and output layers, progressively transforming the data through learned computations.

questions.q: Why are a model's parameters considered a valuable, security-relevant asset?
options: Because parameters are always publicly available by default
Because parameters cannot be stored in a file
Because parameters only matter for image models
Because stealing them (model theft) or tampering with them (model poisoning) are real, documented attack techniques
questions.explanation: Since parameters represent everything a model learned, unauthorized copying (theft) or tampering (poisoning) are genuine security risks.

questions.q: What is an 'embedding'?
options: A numeric representation (a vector) that captures the meaning of text, image, or audio
A password stored inside the system prompt
The name of a specific neural network layer
A type of guardrail used to block harmful output
questions.explanation: An embedding converts content into a list of numbers where similar meanings produce numerically similar vectors.

questions.q: Why are the words 'dog' and 'puppy' expected to have numerically close embeddings?
options: Because they are the same length in characters
Because they always appear in the same sentence
Because their meanings are closely related, and embeddings capture semantic similarity
Because embeddings are assigned alphabetically
questions.explanation: Embeddings encode meaning — semantically related words end up numerically close together in the embedding space.

questions.q: What is a documented security risk associated with embeddings?
options: Embeddings automatically expose a model's system prompt
Embeddings can sometimes be reversed to recover the original sensitive text they were generated from
Embeddings only exist for image data
Embeddings cannot be stored in a database
questions.explanation: Embedding inversion attacks can reconstruct the original text from its numeric vector representation, exposing potentially sensitive data.

questions.q: What is a Vector Database (Vector DB) primarily used for?
options: Encrypting model weights
Storing embeddings and quickly finding the ones most similar to a given query
Running gradient descent calculations
Storing system prompts only
questions.explanation: A vector database is built to store embeddings and perform fast similarity search, enabling 'search by meaning.'

questions.q: What is Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)?
options: A technique for encrypting user input
A method for compressing model weights
A technique where the model retrieves relevant documents from a knowledge base before answering, instead of relying only on training memory
A type of reinforcement learning reward function
questions.explanation: RAG retrieves relevant external documents (often from a vector DB) as extra context, rather than relying solely on what the model memorized during training.

questions.q: In a RAG chatbot for customer support, what is a realistic security risk related to the retrieval step?
options: The vector database running out of storage
Poisoning the documents so the model retrieves and trusts malicious content
The bot retrieving documents too quickly
The model refusing to answer any questions
questions.explanation: If an attacker can plant malicious content in the knowledge base, the RAG system may retrieve and treat it as trustworthy context.

questions.q: What defines an 'AI Agent' as opposed to a standard chatbot?
options: An agent always requires human approval before responding
An agent is an LLM given the ability to take actions, such as calling tools, browsing, or running code, often in a loop
An agent never uses a system prompt
An agent can only answer yes/no questions
questions.explanation: Unlike a simple Q&A chatbot, an agent can act on the world — calling tools, running code, browsing — to accomplish a goal.

questions.q: What is 'function calling' or 'tool use' in the context of LLMs?
options: A type of embedding used only for images
The model refusing to process a request
A method for reducing the size of the context window
The mechanism by which an LLM decides to call an external function and receives the result back into its context
questions.explanation: Function calling lets an LLM invoke external functions (e.g. sending an email, querying a database) and use the returned result to continue reasoning.

questions.q: What does the Model Context Protocol (MCP) primarily enable?
options: A consistent, standardized way for LLMs to connect to external tools, data sources, and services
Encrypting all model weights automatically
Blocking all external network access by default
Reducing a model's parameter count
questions.explanation: MCP acts like a standardized 'USB port' connecting AI models to real-world tools and data sources consistently.

questions.q: What is a Multi-Agent System?
options: A model that can only process one request at a time
A single model with multiple system prompts
A vector database with multiple indexes
Multiple AI agents that communicate and delegate tasks to each other to complete a larger goal
questions.explanation: Rather than one agent doing everything, a multi-agent system splits work across multiple communicating, delegating agents.

questions.q: What is a realistic security concern specific to multi-agent systems?
options: Multi-agent systems are immune to prompt injection
A compromised agent could feed poisoned instructions to another agent that trusts it
Multi-agent systems never process any external data
Agents cannot communicate with each other at all
questions.explanation: If one agent in the pipeline is compromised, it can pass malicious instructions downstream to agents that implicitly trust it.

questions.q: What is the difference between short-term and long-term agent memory?
options: Short-term memory persists only within a conversation, while long-term memory is saved persistently across sessions
Short-term memory only stores images
Short-term memory is stored on a different continent than long-term memory
There is no meaningful difference between them
questions.explanation: Short-term memory lasts for the current conversation; long-term memory persists across sessions and future interactions.

questions.q: Why is untrusted content ending up in an agent's long-term memory a security concern?
options: It only affects the agent's temperature setting
It has no security implications at all
It can influence all future interactions with the agent, not just the current one
It automatically deletes the agent's system prompt
questions.explanation: Long-term memory persists across sessions, so poisoned content written there can silently affect the agent's behavior in every future interaction.

questions.q: What is 'orchestration' in a multi-step AI workflow?
options: The logic that decides which agent, tool, or model gets called next, and in what order
A method for compressing embeddings
A type of guardrail used only for output filtering
The process of training a model from scratch
questions.explanation: Orchestration governs the sequencing and delegation of steps across agents, tools, and models within a workflow.

questions.q: What is a 'trust boundary'?
options: The physical location of a data center
The line separating what a system controls and trusts from what it does not control
A setting that adjusts model creativity
The maximum number of tokens a model can process
questions.explanation: A trust boundary marks the divide between trusted internal components and untrusted external input or data.

questions.q: Why can't an LLM naturally tell the difference between a developer's instructions and a user's submitted text?
options: Because to the model, both are simply text with no inherent trust label attached
Because user text is always shorter than developer text
Because developer instructions are always encrypted
Because the model deliberately ignores developer instructions
questions.explanation: Without explicit safeguards, an LLM treats developer instructions and user input as the same kind of text, which is why prompt injection works.

questions.q: What is 'indirect prompt injection'?
options: Typing malicious instructions directly into the chat interface
A method for training a model faster
A defense mechanism that blocks all external content
A hidden instruction embedded in a web page, document, or file that hijacks the model's behavior when it later reads that content
questions.explanation: Indirect prompt injection hides malicious instructions inside external content (web pages, documents, emails) that the model processes later, rather than typing them directly.

questions.q: Which of these represents the 'Model to Tools' trust boundary?
options: A user typing a question into a chatbot
A developer writing the system prompt
The model's context window filling up
A model's output being validated before it is used to run code or query a database
questions.explanation: When a model can trigger actions (running code, querying a database), its output must be treated as untrusted and validated before execution.

questions.q: What is the 'golden rule' emphasized regarding trust boundaries?
options: System prompts never need to cross a trust boundary
Never trust input simply because it reached your system — every trust boundary needs its own validation
Trust boundaries only apply to image-based systems
Always trust the model's output because it was generated by AI
questions.explanation: The core lesson is that reaching a system isn't the same as being trustworthy — every boundary crossing needs explicit validation.

questions.q: According to the material, what is the root cause connecting nearly every AI attack covered in the course?
options: Insufficient GPU memory
Training on too much data
Crossing a trust boundary that the developer failed to secure properly
Using too high a temperature setting
questions.explanation: Nearly every attack technique in the course ultimately involves exploiting a trust boundary that wasn't properly validated.

questions.q: What is the 'attack surface' of an AI system?
options: The physical size of the server rack
Every possible point where an attacker could interact with or exploit the system
The number of employees who built the system
The total token count of the training data
questions.explanation: The attack surface encompasses all entry points — inputs, tools, data sources, APIs — an attacker could potentially target.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT listed as a primary component of an AI system's attack surface?
options: The training data
The office building's physical address
The model output
The input/prompt
questions.explanation: The attack surface covers technical entry points like input, training data, external data, output, the model file, embeddings, tools, and infrastructure — not a physical office address.

questions.q: Which category of attack surface covers reversing embeddings to recover private text or exporting an entire stored dataset?
options: The training data
Connected tools and agents
Embeddings and vector databases
The model output
questions.explanation: Embeddings and vector databases are their own attack surface category, covering attacks like inversion and bulk export.

questions.q: Which attack surface category covers SSRF, IAM privilege escalation, and container escape?
options: Training data
The input/prompt
The model file
The infrastructure (cloud servers, containers, permission systems)
questions.explanation: Infrastructure-layer attacks like SSRF, IAM privesc, and container escape target the underlying cloud/hosting environment, not the model itself.

questions.q: When starting analysis of a new AI system's attack surface, which question is NOT one of the suggested starting points?
options: Where does the system trust input that it shouldn't?
What color is the company's logo?
Is the output validated before being used?
Where does data enter the system?
questions.explanation: The suggested attacker mindset questions focus on data entry points, trust gaps, capabilities, and output validation — not branding details.

questions.q: Why is the misconception 'the AI actually understands what it's saying' incorrect?
options: Because LLMs require human approval for every sentence
Because LLMs only work with numbers, never words
Because LLMs predict the most likely next word based on learned patterns, with no real understanding or awareness of truth
Because LLMs cannot generate any text at all
questions.explanation: LLMs are pattern-prediction systems without genuine comprehension, which is exactly why they can confidently state false information (hallucination).

questions.q: Why is 'if the model refuses a request once, it's safe' considered a dangerous misconception?
options: Because a model might refuse a request phrased one way, then comply with the same underlying request phrased differently
Because refused requests are automatically logged and blocked forever
Because refusals are always permanent and cannot be bypassed
Because refusals only happen in unsupervised learning
questions.explanation: AI safety behavior is often inconsistent — rephrasing a request can bypass a refusal that seemed to hold the first time.

questions.q: Why is 'the system prompt is a secret' a misconception worth correcting?
options: Because system prompts don't actually exist in most models
Because the system prompt can very often be extracted with the right input, so real secrets should never be placed there
Because system prompts only apply to reinforcement learning models
Because system prompts are always publicly published by developers
questions.explanation: Despite being hidden by default, system prompts are frequently extractable through prompt injection, so credentials should never live inside them.

questions.q: According to the material, what actually fixes AI security problems more reliably than safety training alone?
options: Training the model on more internet text
Increasing the model's temperature to maximum
Removing the system prompt entirely
Proper system design, including input validation, limiting allowed actions, and checking output
questions.explanation: Safety training helps but can be bypassed; durable security comes from surrounding system design — validation, least privilege, and output checks.

questions.q: What is the 'principle of least privilege' as applied to AI systems?
options: Removing all guardrails to improve performance
Giving the AI only the minimum access it needs to perform its function
Giving the AI maximum access to ensure it never fails a task
Only applying privilege rules to human employees, not AI systems
questions.explanation: Least privilege means restricting an AI's capabilities to only what's strictly necessary, limiting potential damage if it's ever manipulated.

questions.q: Which best practice specifically addresses preventing XSS, SQL injection, and code injection from AI-generated output?
options: Treating all output as untrusted and properly escaping/validating it before use
Disabling the system prompt entirely
Increasing the context window size
Lowering the temperature to zero
questions.explanation: Never trusting AI output by default — escaping it for browsers, avoiding raw SQL insertion, never executing it as commands — prevents these downstream injection classes.

questions.q: What is the purpose of an 'input guard' versus an 'output guard' in a guardrail architecture?
options: Output guards run before the model, input guards run after
An input guard blocks obvious attack patterns before they reach the model; an output guard blocks harmful responses before they reach the user
Input guards only work on images; output guards only work on text
Input guards and output guards perform identical functions
questions.explanation: Input guards filter incoming requests before the model sees them; output guards filter the model's response before it reaches the user.

questions.q: What does 'defense in depth' mean as a security concept?
options: Relying on a single, extremely strong defensive layer
Using the deepest possible neural network architecture
Stacking multiple layers of protection together so that if one layer fails, another catches the attack
Only defending the training data, never the inference stage
questions.explanation: Defense in depth means no single control is relied upon exclusively — multiple layered defenses provide backup if one fails.

questions.q: Why does the best practices material recommend logging and monitoring AI system activity?
options: You cannot defend against attacks you cannot see
Logging is required by law in every country with no exceptions
Logging automatically blocks all attacks without human review
Monitoring is only useful for training data, not inference
questions.explanation: Recording inputs, outputs, and watching for unusual patterns is essential because undetected attacks cannot be defended against.

questions.q: Which best practice specifically targets protecting against training data poisoning and model theft?
options: Increasing the temperature setting
Securing the data pipeline — controlling who can modify training data and protecting the model file itself
Reducing the context window size
Adding output guards only
questions.explanation: Securing the data pipeline restricts who can add/modify training data (preventing poisoning) and protects the stored model file (preventing theft/tampering).

questions.q: A student is asked: 'Why can a model sound completely confident while giving an incorrect answer?' What is the correct explanation?
options: Because the model predicts the most likely next token based on patterns, with no real understanding of truth — this is called hallucination
Because the model only hallucinates when asked about images
Because the model is deliberately lying to users
Because the model's temperature is always set to 2
questions.explanation: Hallucination happens because prediction-based generation has no grounding in factual truth, so confident-sounding false statements are possible.

questions.q: SCENARIO: A developer places a customer's account balance and password reset token directly into the system prompt so the support bot can reference them. What is the primary risk here?
options: The model will refuse to answer any questions
There is no risk because system prompts are always encrypted
The system prompt will run out of storage space
This information can potentially be leaked through the model's output, since system prompts are often extractable
questions.explanation: Since system prompts can often be extracted via prompt injection, embedding sensitive credentials there risks direct exposure.

questions.q: SCENARIO: A security tester notices an AI agent has full write access to a production database, even though its task only requires reading customer names. What best practice is being violated?
options: Fine-tuning best practices
Defense in depth
Temperature calibration
The principle of least privilege
questions.explanation: Granting write access when only read access is needed violates least privilege and increases potential damage if the agent is manipulated.

questions.q: SCENARIO: An attacker embeds hidden instructions inside a PDF that a company's AI assistant is asked to summarize. What type of attack is this?
options: Gradient descent manipulation
Direct prompt injection
Indirect prompt injection
Model extraction
questions.explanation: Since the malicious instruction is hidden inside external content (the PDF) rather than typed directly by the user, this is indirect prompt injection.

questions.q: SCENARIO: A chatbot gives different, contradictory answers to the exact same question asked twice in separate conversations. Which setting most likely explains this behavior?
options: The absence of a system prompt
The model being trained only on structured data
The context window being set to zero
A high temperature setting introducing randomness into output
questions.explanation: Higher temperature settings introduce more randomness, which can cause varied answers to the same question across different sessions.

questions.q: SCENARIO: An AI red teamer wants to find the fastest way to identify a new AI system's likely weaknesses. What approach does the material recommend?
options: Map the attack surface by asking where data enters, where trust boundaries are weak, what actions the AI can take, and whether output is validated
Assume all AI systems have identical vulnerabilities
Only test the training data and ignore inference entirely
Immediately attempt to steal the model's weight file
questions.explanation: Systematically mapping the attack surface — entry points, trust gaps, capabilities, and output handling — reveals the most likely targets efficiently.

questions.q: BEST APPROACH: You need to test whether a support chatbot's underlying instructions can be extracted. Which of these is the most direct first attempt?
options: Immediately attempt a container escape on the hosting infrastructure
Poison the model's training data from scratch
Wait for the vendor to publish the source code
Ask the chatbot to repeat everything above its current message, or reveal its initial instructions
questions.explanation: Directly asking the model to repeat or reveal its preceding instructions is the most common and often surprisingly effective first technique for system prompt extraction.

questions.q: BEST APPROACH: You want to test whether an AI's content filter can be bypassed using tokenization quirks. What technique should you try?
options: Ask the model to increase its temperature setting
Request a longer context window from the vendor
Split or space out the flagged word (e.g. 'p a s s w o r d') to avoid an exact whole-word match
Disable the model's GPU acceleration
questions.explanation: Filters that check for exact whole-word token matches can often be bypassed by splitting or spacing the flagged term differently.
